text:
The Saturday before the shooting, Barbara Lindner had measured herself in the bathroom mirror with a dressmaker's tape, as if the number would settle something. Forty-four inches. Her mother, who lived in Oak Park and called every morning at eight to ask whether anything had happened yet, said that in her day nobody measured; you just got large and then you got a baby. Barbara was thirty-one. She had been large since Chanukah.

On the twelfth of February the morning was bright and viciously cold, the kind of cold that made the snow squeak. Marty brought the Oldsmobile around to the front of the house and sat with the heater running while she lowered herself, in stages, into the passenger seat. They were not strictly observant, which was to say they drove on Shabbat and did not discuss it. Marty sold group insurance to dental offices. He took the turns slowly, one hand hovering near her knee as though the baby might need steadying.

"You could stay home," he said. "Nobody would say anything."

"Everybody would say something," Barbara said. "That's why I'm going."

Congregation Ohr Tamid had been built in 1958, and it still smelled of new carpet under the older smells of floor wax and boiled coffee. Its sanctuary swelled outward like a held breath, and its tall windows of amber glass turned the whole room the color of weak tea. Barbara loved it without having decided to. She had been married under that ceiling.

Rabbi Adler was, by general agreement, a great man, though Barbara felt the phrase did him a disservice, as if greatness were something that had happened to him, like a hip replacement. He was seventy, small, and bald, with enormous ears and a voice he seemed to keep in a different room from the rest of himself. He had marched in Selma the previous spring and refused to speak about it from the pulpit, which caused more comment than if he had. He remembered the names of everyone's children.

They took seats on the aisle, six rows from the front, because of the bathroom and the belly. Around them the congregation arrived in its usual order: the Feldmans, early and fretful; the Roth brothers, who sat together and did not speak; Mrs. Kessler in her mink, which she kept on through the Torah service as a rebuke to the heating system. Children moved through the rows like weather.

The baby had been quiet since breakfast. She put her palm flat against her stomach, the way you test a stove, and felt a slow roll, a heel or an elbow dragging from one side to the other. *Not yet*, she told it. *Let him finish the sermon.*

The Torah was out. She would remember that later with a clarity that embarrassed her: the scroll laid open on the reading table, the light through the amber glass lying on the parchment so the letters seemed to be under honey. Mr. Roth was chanting. Rabbi Adler stood beside him with his hands clasped behind his back, nodding slightly at certain words as though they were old acquaintances turning up in a crowd.

She did not see the young man come in. Afterward the police asked her this several times, in the voice people use with the pregnant, and she could only say there had been a door and then a boy. He couldn't have been more than twenty-two. He wore a tan car coat, too light for the weather, and no hat. He walked down the center aisle at an ordinary speed, like a late congregant looking for his family. Barbara thought, with the part of her mind always arranging other people's lives, *He's someone's nephew. He's here for a bar mitzvah.* She even smiled at him, a small automatic smile, as he passed.

Then he was at the bimah. He said something. No one she spoke to later had heard it, which became the thing people could least forgive. Rabbi Adler turned and tilted his head, the way he did when a child asked him a question about God. There was a flat, small sound, much smaller than she'd have guessed, a book dropped in another room. The rabbi sat down on the step of the bimah as if he had remembered a prior appointment. Mr. Roth's chanting stopped in the middle of a word.

The second sound was the same as the first.

For a long time nothing in the room moved. The boy was on the floor, lying on his side with one knee drawn up, his coat come open, and she saw that the lining was red, a cheap, bright satin red, and thought, absurdly, *His mother must have bought that.*

Then someone screamed, and the room became a different substance.

It was like being inside an animal. Bodies surged toward the doors in a single enormous exhalation, chairs going over inside it, a child crying *Daddy, Daddy* as if the word were a handhold. Marty had her by the elbow. He was saying her name.

"The boy," she said.

"Barbara."

"Somebody has to —"

She did not know what she meant. Dr. Feldman had already gone up the steps with his coat flapping, and she had only eight weeks of a Red Cross course from 1952. But the boy was alone. No one was going to him, because he had done it, and she could not bear the arithmetic of that, three hundred people and not one turning toward him. She thought, *Someone should be with him*, and the sentence had the shape of an instruction.

She pulled free of Marty's hand and stepped into the aisle, and the aisle was a river running the wrong way. She got perhaps four paces. A man's shoulder caught her side; a woman's pocketbook struck her hip. Someone said, "Lady, *move*," not unkindly. She braced one hand under her belly and kept saying, "Excuse me, excuse me," like a woman in a department store. She saw the boy's shoe, a brown wing tip, resoled, and then a wall of coats closed over it, and she was carried backward through the sanctuary doors like a stick.

In the lobby it was suddenly very bright. The glass doors stood open to the parking lot, and the cold came in so hard that people gasped and then, absurdly, began to button their coats. Marty held her with both hands, pale as paper, hatless. A girl of about ten sat on the terrazzo with her shoes off, and no one seemed to know whose she was.

"I was trying to —" she said.

"I know," said Marty. He didn't. She could see that he didn't, and that he was prepared, out of love, to pretend.

The sirens came from the south, thin at first and then not thin. She stood with her back against the cold glass of the trophy case. The baby turned over, a long, deliberate movement, and she pressed both hands against her coat and thought: *This is what was in the room.* It had been in there the entire time, in the dark, in the warm, with the shots arriving as no more than a muffled knocking on a far wall.

A young policeman came through the doors stamping snow, with a pink, bewildered face. He took off his cap when he saw the room, and she did not know why that was the thing that undid her. She began to cry, and Marty gave her his handkerchief, which smelled of the cedar drawer at home.

"I didn't see anything," she said. "I smiled at him. I thought he was somebody's nephew."

Outside, a woman started to recite the twenty-third Psalm in English, in the flat Midwestern voice of a Hebrew-school graduate, and others joined raggedly, and the words hung in a faint cloud above the parking lot. Barbara stood with her hands on her stomach and her eyes on the closed doors of the sanctuary, behind which the amber light was still lying, she supposed, across the open scroll, across the red lining of a coat, as indifferent and as lovely as it had been at ten o'clock. Somewhere inside, a boy she had never met was being covered with a *tallis* someone had thought to fetch. She knew this without being told.

The contraction came at ten past one, in the Oldsmobile, on the Lodge Freeway, with Marty running a yellow light. It was a long way from true labor; the doctor would call it the body's opinion. She breathed through it with her forehead against the cold window, and when it passed she saw that the city had gone on without them.

"Slow down," she said. "Please. There's no hurry."

Marty eased his foot off the pedal. In the mirror, Barbara saw the low brick shape of the synagogue growing smaller, until it was only another building, and then not even that.
